stemMd: What is the main purpose of the last paragraph of the passage?

options.label: A
options.textMd: To argue that certification schemes should be abolished.

options.label: B
options.textMd: To show that the remedy described earlier has costs that fall unevenly and may change who sells oil.

options.label: C
options.textMd: To describe a second remedy that avoids the drawbacks of the first.

options.label: D
options.textMd: To restate the problem of unobservable quality described in the second paragraph.

options.label: E
options.textMd: To explain why shoppers in general prefer variety to certainty.

explanationMd:
A purpose question asks what a part of the text is doing, not what it says. Note how the paragraph begins: "The remedy has a price of its own, and it is not paid equally." "The remedy" points back to the tasting panel and label of the third paragraph. The rest of the paragraph shows why the cost is unequal (a large producer spreads it over many bottles; a family with two hundred trees cannot) and what followed in several districts: a higher average price for good oil and fewer independent producers selling it.

So the paragraph complicates the earlier picture: the remedy helps buyers but carries costs that fall unevenly and change who sells oil. It does not call for scrapping the scheme (the last sentence leaves the verdict to shoppers), it adds no second remedy, it does not return to the original problem, and it does not say which of certainty or variety shoppers prefer.

distractorRationale.a: The paragraph reports costs and a trade-off and ends by leaving the judgement open, so it does not argue for abolition.
distractorRationale.d: The paragraph turns to a different subject: the costs of the remedy, not the original problem.
distractorRationale.c: No second remedy is introduced; the paragraph examines the drawbacks of the first.
distractorRationale.e: The paragraph says only that the answer depends on which of the two shoppers value more. It does not say which they prefer.

accessibilityText: A purpose-and-structure question about the olive oil passage. It asks for the main purpose of the last paragraph. The five choices: to argue that certification schemes should be abolished; to show that the remedy described earlier has costs that fall unevenly and may change who sells oil; to describe a second remedy that avoids the drawbacks of the first; to restate the problem of unobservable quality from the second paragraph; to explain why shoppers in general prefer variety to certainty.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.

review.author: tolc-e-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The last paragraph says the remedy has costs that are not paid equally, that these costs favour large producers, and that certification reduced the number of independent sellers. A overstates, since the author stays neutral. C is wrong because no second remedy is described. D is wrong because the paragraph adds new content. E is wrong because the author leaves the preference open. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolce-verbal-run2) reached the same answer: The last paragraph says the remedy has costs that are 'not paid equally', since large producers spread them over many bottles and small ones cannot. It also says certification reduced the number of independent producers. A is wrong because the paragraph describes costs and does not call for abolition. C is wrong because no second remedy appears. D is wrong because the paragraph makes new points. E is contradicted: the label 'cannot answer' whether shoppers prefer certainty or variety.]
